idiom_name: factory interface implemented by object literals; DI token/provider for selection
implementation_notes: An interface with one method per product kind, implemented by plain objects, is the TypeScript realization: the concrete factory is a value, not a class, and structural typing checks each object against the interface at compile time. When the family must be injected rather than imported - or when interfaces have no runtime representation - use a DI token with a factory provider (Angular's InjectionToken + useFactory) so the container owns selection. A discriminated union of family keys with an exhaustive switch is the zero-framework alternative; keep products as interfaces/types so consumers never import a concrete family module. TypeScript's `satisfies` operator (TS 4.9+) can verify that a factory object satisfies the interface without widening the type, catching missing methods at compile time.
pitfalls: Structural typing is not nominal: any object with matching members satisfies UIFactory, so an unrelated component factory can be injected by mistake - brand the interface or add a discriminator field when families must be distinguished.
Interfaces disappear at runtime, so they cannot be DI tokens; tokens must be InjectionToken instances (matching the same instance everywhere, or DI reports a NullInjectorError).
A module-level object factory closing over request-scoped state shares it across requests; create the factory per request or inject the state.
Using `as` casts to force a wrong-shaped factory bypasses type checking; prefer a `assertFactory(f: UIFactory)` helper that validates at least one method name to make accidental mismatches visible.
